evidence: Sen. Ep. 24.26: aestās in autumnum dēsinit
Sall. J. 83.2: omne bellum sūmī facile, cēterum aegerrumē dēsinere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of things coming to an end; Lewis & Short find this use “not frequent till after the Augustan period”, though Sallust and Ovid have it (dēsierant imbrēs, Ov. Met. 5.285). The same verb as stop (cease).

terms.gloss: come to an end, have an end
evidence: Ov. F. 5.602: tepidī fīnem tempora vēris habent

terms.gloss: run out, end (of a period of time)
evidence: Cic. Div. 1.53: quīntō annō exeunte (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of time running out: a year, a truce, the holidays; hieme exeunte, at the end of winter.

phrases.latin: diem nox premit, diēs noctem, aestās in autumnum dēsinit, autumnō hiemps īnstat, quae vēre compescitur; omnia sīc trānseunt ut revertantur
phrases.english: night presses on day and day on night; summer ends in autumn, winter follows hard on autumn and is checked by spring; everything passes only to come back

phrases.latin: nihil est aut certē exiguum est; dūrēmus; jam dēsinet
phrases.english: It’s nothing, or very little anyway; let’s hold on; it will soon be over

phrases.latin: tum mihi nōn dubiīs auctōribus incipit aestās, et tepidī fīnem tempora vēris habent
phrases.english: then, on good authority, summer begins for me, and the season of warm spring comes to an end
